title: Membranes and membrane transport
summary: How the phospholipid bilayer acts as a barrier, and how diffusion, osmosis, channels and pumps move substances across it. HL adds membrane fluidity, gated channels, the sodium–potassium pump, cotransport and cell adhesion.

keyterms.definition: Double layer of phospholipids with hydrophilic heads facing out and a hydrophobic core; a barrier to ions and polar molecules.
Passive net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration directly through the phospholipid bilayer, e.g. oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Passive net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a region of lower to higher solute concentration.
Integral channel protein that greatly increases a membrane's permeability to water.
Integral proteins are embedded in one or both lipid layers; peripheral proteins are attached to the membrane surface.
Passive movement of particles down their concentration gradient through membrane proteins such as channel proteins.
Integral protein with a hydrophilic pore through which specific ions or molecules diffuse; the pore's size and charge make it selective.
Movement of particles against their concentration gradient by pump proteins, using energy from ATP; pumps move particles in one direction only.
Membrane proteins or lipids with carbohydrate chains on the extracellular side; involved in cell recognition and adhesion.
Model of membrane structure: a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in or attached to it, in a mosaic pattern.
Lipid in animal cell membranes that modulates fluidity; its hydroxyl group lies among the phospholipid heads.
Bulk transport using vesicles: endocytosis takes material in by membrane fission; exocytosis releases it by vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane.
Channel that opens or closes in response to a stimulus: neurotransmitter-gated (e.g. nicotinic acetylcholine receptor) or voltage-gated (e.g. Na+ and K+ channels in axons).
Exchange transporter that uses one ATP to pump three Na+ out of and two K+ into the cell.
Indirect active transport: Na+ diffusing in down its gradient carries glucose in against its gradient, e.g. in small intestine and kidney.
Membrane proteins that bind cells to each other to form tissues; different CAMs form different types of cell–cell junction.

questions.prompt: Why is a phospholipid bilayer a barrier to ions and large polar molecules?
options: The phosphate heads are positively charged and repel all ions
The bilayer has no gaps between phospholipids
Its hydrophobic core of fatty acid tails does not let hydrophilic particles pass easily
Ions are too large to fit between phospholipids
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic particles are strongly attracted to water and cannot easily enter the non-polar interior of the bilayer, so permeability to them is very low. Small ions are tiny; it is their charge, not size, that blocks them.

questions.statement: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross membranes by simple diffusion between the phospholipids.
questions.explanation: They are small and non-polar, so they pass through the hydrophobic core without a transport protein, down their concentration gradients.

questions.text: The net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane towards a higher solute concentration is called ___.
questions.explanation: In osmosis water moves passively from lower to higher solute concentration, because solutes reduce the concentration of free water molecules.

questions.prompt: Which of these would cross a pure phospholipid bilayer least readily?
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Testosterone
Sodium ions
questions.explanation: Charged ions such as Na+ are hydrophilic and surrounded by water, so they barely enter the hydrophobic core. Small non-polar gases and steroids diffuse through readily.

questions.statement: Simple diffusion requires energy from ATP.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive: it results from random motion of particles and only occurs down a concentration gradient, so no ATP is needed.

questions.text: Channel proteins called ___ greatly increase the permeability of membranes to water.
questions.explanation: Some water crosses the bilayer directly, but aquaporins let water pass far faster, e.g. in kidney collecting ducts and root cells.

questions.prompt: Match each substance to the main way it crosses the plasma membrane.
questions.explanation: Small non-polar molecules and steroids cross the bilayer directly; water and ions depend mainly on proteins that provide hydrophilic routes.

questions.prompt: An animal cell with a cytoplasm of higher solute concentration than the surrounding solution is placed in that solution. What happens?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis and it shrinks
Water enters the cell by osmosis and it swells
Solutes are actively pumped in until concentrations are equal
There is no net movement of water
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis towards the higher solute concentration, which is inside the cell, so it swells and may burst because animal cells have no cell wall.

questions.prompt: Which change would increase the rate of simple diffusion of oxygen into a cell?
options: A steeper concentration gradient across the membrane
Adding more ATP to the cell
Adding more pump proteins to the membrane
A thicker membrane
questions.explanation: Net diffusion is faster when the concentration difference is greater or the distance is shorter. ATP and pumps play no part in simple diffusion.

questions.prompt: Put the layers in order, going from outside the cell to inside.
items: Hydrophilic heads of the outer layer
Hydrophobic core of fatty acid tails
Hydrophilic heads of the inner layer
questions.explanation: The phospholipid heads face the watery fluid on both sides, and the tails of both layers meet in the middle to form the hydrophobic core.

lessons.title: Membrane proteins and the fluid mosaic model

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an integral membrane protein from a peripheral one?
options: Integral proteins are always glycoproteins
Integral proteins are embedded in the hydrophobic core of one or both lipid layers; peripheral proteins are attached to the surface
Peripheral proteins span the whole membrane
Peripheral proteins are found only on the inner surface
questions.explanation: Integral proteins have hydrophobic regions that sit within the bilayer; peripheral proteins are attached to the surface, often to integral proteins, and do not enter the core.

questions.statement: Facilitated diffusion through a channel protein can move ions against their concentration gradient.
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive, so it can only move particles down their concentration gradient. Moving against a gradient needs active transport by a pump.

questions.text: Pump proteins use energy from ___ to move particles against their concentration gradient.
questions.explanation: Pumps hydrolyse ATP and use the energy released to change shape, carrying particles from lower to higher concentration.

questions.prompt: What makes a channel protein selective for particular ions?
options: It uses ATP to reject the wrong ions
It only opens when the concentration gradient reverses
It binds every ion briefly and releases only the correct one using energy
The diameter of its pore and the chemical properties of the amino acids lining it
questions.explanation: Only particles of the right size and charge fit through the hydrophilic pore, so each channel type is specific. No energy is involved.

questions.prompt: Match each transport process to its description.

pairs.right: Passive, through bilayer, no protein needed
Passive, down gradient, through channel proteins
Against gradient by pumps using ATP
Passive water movement towards higher solute concentration

questions.explanation: Only active transport uses ATP and works against a gradient; the other three are passive and differ in what moves and whether a protein is needed.

questions.statement: Glycoproteins and glycolipids have their carbohydrate chains on the extracellular side, where they function in cell recognition and adhesion.
questions.explanation: The carbohydrate parts form a coat (glycocalyx) on the outer surface that other cells and molecules can bind to and recognize.

questions.text: The ___ model describes the membrane as a fluid bilayer with proteins embedded in it in a mosaic pattern.
questions.explanation: Lipids and many proteins can move laterally (fluid), and the scattered proteins form a mosaic. The older Davson–Danielli model placed protein layers on both surfaces.

questions.prompt: Why is permeability by simple diffusion described as not selective?
options: It allows every substance to cross at the same rate
It is controlled by channel proteins that open at random
It depends only on particle size and hydrophobicity, so the cell cannot control which particles cross
It needs ATP, which is used non-specifically
questions.explanation: Any small or hydrophobic particle can diffuse through the bilayer. Selectivity comes from proteins: specific channels and pumps decide which ions and polar molecules cross.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes pump proteins from channel proteins?
options: Pumps use energy to change conformation and move particles in one direction only, even against a gradient
Pumps are peripheral proteins whereas channels are integral
Pumps allow water through while channels allow ions through
Pumps work faster than channels because they use ATP
questions.explanation: Pumps are integral proteins that use ATP to change shape and move particles one way against a gradient. Channels are passive pores and are usually much faster.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of active transport by a pump protein in order.
items: The particle binds to the pump on one side of the membrane
ATP is used and the pump changes conformation
The particle is released on the other side
The pump returns to its original conformation
questions.explanation: Energy from ATP drives a shape change that moves the bound particle across, after which the pump resets ready for the next cycle.

questions.prompt: Organisms living in cold environments often have more unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes. Why?
options: Unsaturated fatty acids make the membrane more rigid, protecting it from ice
Unsaturated fatty acids release heat when they bond
Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, keeping the membrane fluid at low temperatures
Unsaturated fatty acids reduce permeability to water
questions.explanation: Kinks in cis-unsaturated tails stop phospholipids packing tightly, so the membrane stays fluid when it is cold. Membranes rich in saturated fatty acids would become too rigid.

questions.statement: Cholesterol in animal cell membranes reduces fluidity at higher temperatures and prevents the membrane becoming too rigid at lower temperatures.
questions.explanation: Cholesterol restricts phospholipid movement when warm but disrupts close packing of tails when cold, so it acts as a fluidity buffer.

questions.text: The hydroxyl group of cholesterol is attracted to the ___ heads of the phospholipids, while the rest of the molecule sits among the tails.
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is mostly hydrophobic but its single –OH is polar, so it orients with the –OH among the heads and its rings among the fatty acid tails.

questions.prompt: Which property of membranes makes endocytosis and exocytosis possible?
options: Fluidity, which lets membranes pinch off to form vesicles and fuse with other membranes
Rigidity, which keeps vesicles spherical
Impermeability to water, which keeps vesicles from bursting
The presence of cell walls around the membrane
questions.explanation: Because the bilayer is fluid, it can bend, separate (fission) to form vesicles in endocytosis, and fuse with the plasma membrane in exocytosis.

questions.prompt: Match each membrane protein to its role.

pairs.right: Channel opened by binding of a neurotransmitter
Opens when the axon membrane depolarizes
Three Na+ out, two K+ in per ATP
Uses the Na+ gradient to bring glucose in

questions.explanation: Gated channels open in response to a ligand or a voltage change; the Na+/K+ pump is an exchange transporter; the cotransporter uses the Na+ gradient the pump creates.

questions.statement: The sodium–potassium pump moves three Na+ into the cell and two K+ out for each ATP used.
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: three Na+ are pumped out and two K+ are pumped in, building the gradients used in nerve impulses and cotransport.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of one sodium–potassium pump cycle in order.
items: Three Na+ bind to the pump from inside the cell
ATP transfers a phosphate to the pump
The pump changes shape and releases Na+ outside
Phosphate is released, the pump returns to its original shape and K+ is released inside
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation by ATP opens the pump to the outside; loss of the phosphate after K+ binds opens it to the inside again.

questions.prompt: Why is glucose uptake by sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters called indirect active transport?
options: The cotransporter hydrolyses ATP directly, but only occasionally
Glucose moves down its own concentration gradient
Glucose enters by osmosis together with water
The Na+ gradient that drives it is created by sodium–potassium pumps using ATP, so the cotransporter itself uses no ATP
questions.explanation: Na+ diffusing in down its gradient provides the energy to carry glucose in against its gradient. ATP is used elsewhere, by the pumps that maintain the Na+ gradient.

questions.text: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters absorb glucose from the small intestine and reabsorb it in the ___ of the kidney.
questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs all filtered glucose; cotransporters let it be taken up even when it is more concentrated inside the cells.

questions.prompt: What is the role of cell adhesion molecules (CAMs)?
options: They pump ions to keep cells the same size
They bind adjacent cells together to form tissues, with different CAMs forming different junction types
They digest the extracellular matrix so cells can move
They are receptors for steroid hormones
questions.explanation: CAMs are membrane proteins that attach cells to one another; different types of CAM are used in different cell–cell junctions.

questions.statement: Exocytosis increases the surface area of the plasma membrane because the vesicle membrane becomes part of it.
questions.explanation: When a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane its phospholipids and proteins are added; endocytosis removes membrane, balancing this.

questions.prompt: What happens when acetylcholine binds to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on a postsynaptic membrane?
options: The receptor hydrolyses ATP to pump Na+ out
Acetylcholine diffuses through the receptor into the cell
The channel opens and positive ions, mainly Na+, diffuse into the cell
The channel closes and the membrane becomes impermeable
questions.explanation: This receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated channel: binding of acetylcholine opens the pore, letting Na+ flow in down its gradient and depolarizing the membrane.
